claims.evidence: Search summary: local anaesthetic, needle between spine bones to collect spinal fluid, pressure may be measured. Purpose of finding a cause or giving treatment not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A lumbar puncture uses a needle in the lower back to collect the fluid around the spinal cord, and the pressure of the fluid may also be measured.

claims.evidence: Usually done in hospital with local anaesthetic; one leaflet says typically 15 to 20 minutes but can be longer, another says 20 to 40 minutes.
claims.newSentence: A lumbar puncture is usually done in hospital under local anaesthetic, and leaflets give different times, from about 15 minutes to 40 minutes.

claims.evidence: Spinal fluid is collected (at least three containers). Giving medicines or anaesthetic into the spine was not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Fluid from around the spinal cord is collected for testing.

claims.evidence: Headache is the most common side effect (supported). 'Very safe' wording appears in NHS 111 Wales text, but a reassurance of safety is not allowed on this site.
claims.newSentence: A headache is the most common side effect, and serious complications are described as extremely rare.

claims.evidence: Some results can come back within a day, others take weeks; some specialist tests up to 10 weeks.
claims.newSentence: Some results come back within a day and others take weeks, so the team can say when to expect them.

claims.evidence: Needle goes between the bones of the spine to collect spinal fluid.
Retrieved text says 'spinal fluid'; the term CSF was not seen. Plain textbook naming.
'The procedure is usually done in hospital.'
Local anaesthetic in the lower back, needle between spine bones, fluid collected.
Only collecting fluid for tests and measuring pressure were retrieved; treating a condition or giving an anaesthetic were not.
claims.newSentence: Doctors use it to collect spinal fluid for testing and to measure the pressure of the fluid.

claims.evidence: No retrieved text on injecting medicines or anaesthetic into the spine.
Doctor may measure the pressure of the fluid. 'Normal range' wording is a reference-range idea, dropped.
claims.newSentence: The pressure of the fluid may also be measured.

claims.evidence: One NHS-hosted leaflet: typically 15 to 20 minutes but can take longer; another trust: 20 to 40 minutes.
claims.newSentence: One leaflet says it typically takes around 15 to 20 minutes but can take longer, and another says 20 to 40 minutes.

claims.evidence: Lower back is cleaned and a local anaesthetic injection is given into the skin.
claims.newSentence: The lower back is cleaned and numbed with a local anaesthetic injection before the needle is placed.

claims.evidence: Staying still not retrieved.
Leaflets say to expect to rest flat for a short period afterwards; details come from the hospital leaflet.
claims.newSentence: Leaflets say to expect to rest flat for a short period afterwards, and the team caring for you gives the details.

claims.evidence: Headache common; back pain and bruising common and usually settle within days. Fluid leak and swelling as listed were not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Headache, back pain and bruising are common side effects.

claims.evidence: Headache is the most frequent side effect.
Can start a few hours to two days after and last for a few days.
Lying flat usually helps; drinking plenty of fluids may lower the chance of a headache.
claims.newSentence: Leaflets say lying flat usually helps the headache.

claims.evidence: 'Usually very safe' appears in NHS 111 Wales summary; site rules bar calling a procedure safe. Retrieved text says complications are extremely rare.
claims.newSentence: Serious complications are described as extremely rare.

claims.evidence: Very rare: infection, bleeding, nerve injury, hearing loss, double vision. Blood clots not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Very rare complications include infection, bleeding, nerve injury, hearing loss and double vision.

claims.evidence: Serious harm from complications occurs in less than 1 in 10,000 lumbar punctures.
Leaflets list severe headache not easing lying flat, fever, neck stiffness, leg weakness or numbness as red flags; route is ward or NHS 111.
claims.newSentence: Leaflets list a severe headache that does not ease on lying flat, a fever, neck stiffness or leg weakness as reasons to get urgent advice from the hospital team or NHS 111.

claims.evidence: Generic site signposting, no clinical claim.

claims.newSentence: Some results can come back within a day.

notes: Only 3 searches used. Search summaries blend pages, so urls are the most plausible source pages, not verified excerpt by excerpt. The author's url https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/lumbar-puncture/ was never returned; nhs.uk/conditions/lumbar-puncture/ was returned instead. The 15 to 20 minute figure was only attributed to 'an NHS-hosted leaflet' in the summary. The nhs.uk page and dgft page were not independently confirmed for c19/c20/c26, which came from blended summaries.
